newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - New sick pay protests hit German firms.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - New sick pay protests hit German firms.

text.p: German companies in the metal, engineering and electronics sectors on Monday suffered a further day of mass protests by workers against planned cuts to sick pay entitlements.
Around 100,000 workers downed tools in the southern state of Bavaria in protests that are scheduled to be followed by demonstrations in other regions of Germany this week.

Leaders of the IG Metall union said the size of the protest, the third such carried out by engineering workers in the last five weeks, showed the continued strength of feeling among workers on the issue.

"We are ready for further industrial action if employers persist in this kamikaze behaviour," IG Metall Bavaria regional chief Werner Neugebauer told a rally outside the Ingolstadt plant of car-maker Volkswagen AG's Audi unit.

Other firms affected by the walk-outs were electronics and engineering groups Siemens AG and AEG AG, both of which have significant operations in Bavaria, and truck manufacturer MAN Nutzfahrzeuge AG in Munich.
The protests came despite promises last month by employers in the sector to hold off implementing a new law cutting sick pay from its current 100 percent of salary to 80 percent.

But negotiators for the employers have made little secret of their wish to include the new law in 1997 wage contracts as part of attempts to reduce labour costs that they say are making Germany internationally uncompetitive.
A spokesman for the federation of Bavarian metal and electronics industry described the protests as "irresponsible and against the law", a charge refuted by IG Metall.

Regional leaders of the union gave notice last month of a decision to cancel existing wage contracts for metal and engineering workers in Bavaria, who make up around a fifth of total employment in the sector.
Such a move means they can carry out full strikes from the end of February if no negotiated deal is reached before then.
Workers in the east German state of Saxony and the Berlin and Brandenburg region are expected to continue the protests in the sector later this week.

The new sick pay law came into force in as part of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's austerity drive aimed at helping Germany fulfil strict fiscal requirements to qualify for a single European currency due for launch in 1999.

Union and employer negotiators are due to meet in the south-western town of Karlsruhe on Thursday in an attempt to find a compromise on wages and labour costs for workers in the state of Baden-Wuerttemberg.
IG Metall representatives have said that the would then decide whether any deal could then be used as a pilot for similar regional agreements across the country.
